# Parking Slot Calculator

ITU coursework, 2018. Restored in 2026: input checks with retry, tests, CI. Original code: tag `original-2018`.

**[Run it online](https://godbolt.)** (Compiler Explorer, no login, example input built in)

## What it does

Finds the parking slot that is furthest from the nearest parked car, measured as Manhattan distance. This is the safest place to park.

## Build and run

```sh
make                         # builds ./parking_slot_calculator
./parking_slot_calculator
make test                    # runs the tests in tests/
```

## Input

| Prompt | Valid | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Size: ` | one whole number, 1-50 | |
| `Cars: ` | one whole number, 0 to size² | size² (full lot) prints `No slot found` and exits, with no location prompts |
| `Locations: ` | two whole numbers `X Y`, each 1 to size | the slot must be free |

A line with extra tokens, non-numbers, or nothing is invalid. The program says why on stderr and asks again. End of input at any prompt prints `error: unexpected end of input` on stderr and exits with status 1.

Prompts and errors go to stderr. The result goes to stdout.

Example session (what you type is after each prompt):

```text
Size: 5
Cars: 2
Locations: 1 1
Locations: 5 5
Best Slot Found In: 1 5
```

## How it works

For every slot, the program checks every other slot for a parked car and keeps the smallest Manhattan distance. It then picks the slot with the largest of these distances. Ties go to the first slot in row-major order. This brute force takes O(n⁴) time for an n x n lot.

What I'd do now: a multi-source BFS that starts from all parked cars at once. It finds every slot's distance to the nearest car in O(n²). I kept the brute force here on purpose: this is a restoration, not a rewrite.
